entry.title: The Phrase That Stayed
entry.content:
I read Skin in the Game in 2022, after The Black Swan and Antifragile, and I will be honest about what is left of it four years later. I could not tell you the order of its chapters or retell most of its stories. What I kept is the phrase. I say “skin in the game” all the time now, at work and outside it, whenever I mean that someone should feel responsible for a thing, own it, dare something, and put enough of themselves into it that it can make the world a little better. If everyone had some skin in the game, I think we would all live in a more engaged world.

That is a strange thing to review, so this is a review of what a book leaves behind. I went back to the text to check whether the phrase I use is the one Taleb meant. It mostly is, but the book is harder than the phrase, and in places better.

I give it 8.5 out of 10. Few books have changed how I talk as much as this one, and it gets more relevant every year that agents take on more of the work.

What Taleb means

The book is the fourth volume of what Taleb calls the Incerto, after Fooled by Randomness, The Black Swan, and Antifragile, and it states its claim early: “skin in the game is necessary for fairness, commercial efficiency, and risk management: skin in the game is necessary to understand the world.” The core is symmetry. Whoever takes a risk should carry its downside, and whoever gains from a decision should be exposed to it when it goes wrong.

He starts, as I remembered, with Hammurabi. The code on the basalt stele in the Louvre, some 3,800 years old, opens its best known rule with “If a builder builds a house and the house collapses and causes the death of the owner of the house”, and the builder pays with his life. Taleb’s point is not the cruelty but the design. The builder knows more about the house than anyone, and the best place to hide a flaw is in the corners only the builder can see. The law makes the builder’s fate depend on what is in those corners. I used that passage before, in The Original Data Company, because insurers live on exactly this problem.

The counterexample is what he calls the Bob Rubin trade. Robert Rubin, a former US Treasury Secretary, “collected more than $120 million in compensation from Citibank in the decade preceding the banking crash of 2008,” and when the bank had to be rescued, “he didn’t write any check.” The upside was private; the downside went to everyone else. From there Taleb draws the sentence about institutions I quote most after the title: “Bureaucracy is a construction by which a person is conveniently separated from the consequences of his or her actions.” (More on that in a note.)

The parts I had forgotten

Rereading, I was surprised how much of the book is not about bankers at all.

Chapter 2, “The Most Intolerant Wins”, argues that a small, stubborn minority, three or four percent of a population, can impose its preferences on everyone if the rule is asymmetric: someone who keeps kosher will not drink non-kosher lemonade, but nobody else minds drinking kosher, so producers and grocers simply make all of it kosher rather than keep two supplies. It is one of the most useful ideas in the book and has little to do with risk in the narrow sense; I applied it to software standards in The most intolerant wins.

Chapter 8 introduces Lindy, named after a New York deli where actors noticed that Broadway shows that had lasted a hundred days could expect a hundred more. Taleb turns it into a rule for anything that does not age: “the only effective judge of things is time”, which is a better test for a framework, a book, or a protocol than any review, this one included. I use it for choosing technology, in Lindy for software.

Chapter 19, “The Logic of Risk Taking”, which Taleb calls the central chapter and puts last, is the one I would send to an engineer. Its argument is about ruin: an average over many people is not the same as the path of one person over time, and a strategy that is rational on paper is irrational if one bad outcome ends the game. “Rationality is avoidance of systemic ruin,” he writes. That is the same idea that runs through The Black Swan and Antifragile, now with a name for the person who has to live with it, and it is the rule I use for gating agents in Rationality is avoidance of ruin.

And there is the tone. Taleb is combative, repeats himself, and has a long chapter on the “Intellectual Yet Idiot” that reads like a settling of scores. Some of the book is more fun to have read than to read. I do not hold that against it; it is part of how the ideas stay with you.

Soul in the game

The surprise was that my own use of the phrase is in the book too, under a different name. Taleb writes of people with “skin in the game (or, better, soul in the game),” and he uses it for something beyond exposure to loss: doing a thing because you care about it, with no one forcing the symmetry. He tells how he learned enough Akkadian to recite Hammurabi’s law in its own sounds, because talking about the stele without being able to read it felt like cheating. He notes that Microsoft, Apple, Facebook, and Google “were started by people with skin and soul in the game.” And in chapter 13 he writes the line I wish I had remembered: “Courage is the only virtue you cannot fake.” It got a note of its own.

That is where I land. Taleb’s version is mostly negative: remove those who can harm others without being harmed. Mine is mostly positive: the people who carry things forward are the ones who put themselves into them, which is what I argued in Who carries progress and saw in a friend’s idea factory. Taleb says the two belong together. The introduction calls skin in the game “mostly about justice, honor, and sacrifice,” and the glossary is blunt: “virtue devoid of courage, sacrifice, and skin in the game is never virtue.” The penalty and the engagement are one idea seen from two sides.

What is left when code is cheap

The reason the phrase matters more to me now than in 2022 is the question everyone in my field is asking since agents started writing software: if code is cheap, what is left? My answer is Taleb’s. Ownership.

Ideas were always cheap. Everyone has one, the way everyone has an opinion, and an idea nobody acts on is worth nothing. Code used to be the expensive part. It took years to learn, it was hard to hire, and harder still to scale a team without losing quality: Fred Brooks put it in The Mythical Man-Month in 1975 as “Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.” That constraint is going away. One person with a fleet of agents can now produce what a department produced, and at the Agentic Engineering Days in Zurich this month the slide that got the room was Krzysztof Cieślak’s “Code is cheap. Shared understanding and trust aren’t” (I wrote about it in The Constraint Moves).

What does not get cheaper is someone with a vision, the endurance to stay loyal to it for years, and the willingness to answer for it. When I choose a product or a service, I am not buying its code. I am buying the knowledge that somebody will keep delivering it next year, and that this somebody will pay, in reputation and if need be in court, when it fails. That is skin in the game in the most ordinary sense, and it is the one thing an agent cannot supply on its own behalf.

Taleb saw half of this coming, from the other side. Chapter 3, “How to Legally Own Another Person”, is about why companies prefer employees to contractors, and his answer is that employees have something to lose: “employees have a reputation to protect.” A firm, in his account, holds its people through their dependence and their reputation, and that is what makes them reliable. An AI agent is the perfect employee in every respect but this one. It has no reputation, no career, nothing to lose. So all of the exposure that used to be spread across a team now flows to the person at the top, as I wrote in The perfect employee has nothing to lose. Whoever runs a thousand agents owns everything they do, in Taleb’s full sense of the word, because there is nobody left below to share it.

That changes what a builder is. The scarce person is no longer the one who can write the code but the one who can be trusted with the outcome: who will be there in five years, who has staked a name on the thing, who has, as Taleb puts it in the introduction, something in the portfolio rather than an opinion: “Don’t tell me what you ‘think,’ just tell me what’s in your portfolio.” Lindy applies here too. A product that has been run well by the same owner for a decade carries more trust than any feature list, because time is the judge that cannot be argued with. In my own work this is the design principle behind every agent platform I build: each action traceable to a person who answers for it, each agent with a human sponsor whose name is on the line. In Hammurabi’s terms, it puts the builder back under the house.

The last owners

I take this one step further than Taleb would. I believe that ownership, trust, and the ability to execute are what remain after AI and robotics have taken over most human labour. If we reach a society of abundance, fully automated, where material and social needs are provided for, it will still need a small group of people who oversee the machines: who decide how energy and resources are allocated, and who keep the whole system running. The ultimate engineer-operator.

The book gives two warnings for that world, and I think they are the right ones. The first is chapter 2: a small minority with soul in the game sets the rules for everyone else, whether or not anyone notices. A tiny group of operators will shape a society the way three percent of kosher drinkers shape the lemonade aisle, so it matters a great deal who they are and what they care about. The second is the oldest rule in the book. The fewer people stand between a decision and its consequences, the more those few must carry them. Bureaucracy, in Taleb’s definition, separates people from the consequences of their actions; a fully automated society would be the largest bureaucracy ever built, unless the people at the top live under the house they built. If there are last owners, they need the most skin in the game of anyone, not the least.

Who should read it

Anyone who has to decide who gets to decide: managers, founders, people who design institutions or systems. Read The Black Swan and Antifragile first if you can; this is the book where their ideas turn into ethics. Skip around if a chapter loses you, and do not skip chapter 19.

I kept one phrase from it for four years and used it more than almost any other idea I have read. That is the best test of a book I know, and Taleb would call it Lindy.

References

  • Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life, Penguin, 2018
  • Fred Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month, 1975, via Brooks’s law
  • Krzysztof Cieślak, closing slide of his talk at Agentic Engineering Days Zurich 2026, in The Constraint Moves

entry.title: Courage is the only virtue you cannot fake
entry.content:
Chapter 13 of Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s Skin in the Game, “The Merchandising of Virtue”, contains the line I wish I had remembered from my first reading: “Courage is the only virtue you cannot fake.” Everything else can be performed. Generosity can be a press release, kindness can be a strategy, an opinion can be shared when it is safe to share. Courage costs something by definition, and the cost is what makes it real.

Taleb’s test for virtue follows from that. “Sticking up for truth when it is unpopular is far more of a virtue, because it costs you something,” he writes, and the price is usually your reputation. Joining a crowd that is already shaming someone is the opposite: safe, popular, and in his words “a mixture of bullying and cowardice.”

The part I keep coming back to is his advice to young people who come to him wanting to reduce poverty or save the world. He gives them three rules:

  1. “Never engage in virtue signaling”
  2. “Never engage in rent-seeking”
  3. “You must start a business. Put yourself on the line, start a business.”

Take bounded risks, he says, and if you get rich, which is optional, spend it generously on others. “Courage (risk taking) is the highest virtue. We need entrepreneurs.”

I agree with this more than with most advice on how to do good. It matches what I believe about who carries progress: not the people with the best intentions about the world in general, but the people who put themselves into one concrete thing and answer for it. It is also what I mean when I say “skin in the game” in everyday speech, as I wrote in my review of the book: ownership, daring, and enough of yourself in something that it can make the world a little better.

entry.title: Small, focused, high-trust
entry.content:
In a 2020 vision memo, written after Microsoft’s investment, Sam Altman warned his own company against growing too large. Karen Hao quotes it in Empire of AI (chapter 11): “what has worked for us so far is being small, focused, high-trust, low-bullshit, and intense.” Too many people and too much bureaucracy, he wrote, “can easily kill great ideas or result in sclerosis”, and OpenAI could fulfil its mission “with a surprisingly small number of great people.”

He meant it. Hao reports that in late 2022, after ChatGPT, when every team was stretched thin and managers begged for head count, Altman kept repeating the line and wanted to add no more than about a hundred people. Other executives wanted closer to five hundred. OpenAI had about 300 people in October 2022, close to 600 by the middle of 2023, and nearly 800 when the board fired Altman that November.

I have made the same observation in every large organisation I have worked in or with, public or private. A group of people has to spend work on holding itself together, and that share grows faster than the group. Fred Brooks put the arithmetic in The Mythical Man-Month: every pair of people is a possible line of communication, and the number of pairs grows with the square of the headcount.

PeoplePairs who may need to talk
510
1045
501,225
500124,750
5,00012,497,500

Nobody talks to everyone, so the organisation adds structure: managers, meetings, processes, reporting lines, approval steps. Each is reasonable. Together they become the leviathan, a body whose main occupation is keeping itself intact, whether it is a ministry or a multinational. Its slowness is the price of its coherence.

What interests me is that the arithmetic may be changing. If a small team with agents can do what used to take a department, the number of people a mission needs drops, and with it the overhead. I wrote about that from the side of the individual in power in the good sense and citizen entrepreneurs. Altman’s “surprisingly small number of great people” reads differently in 2026 than it did in 2020.

Small has its own failure mode, and Hao’s account shows it too: teams stretched so thin that the people in them burn out. Small, focused, and high-trust is a discipline, and OpenAI could not keep it. Neither, as far as I know, has anyone else at that scale.

Related: A billion without a plan, and my review of the book, An Empire of People.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 11, “Apex”.
  • Frederick P. Brooks Jr., The Mythical Man-Month (1975), chapter 2.

entry.title: Something closer to a religion
entry.content:
Karen Hao opens Empire of AI with two epigraphs. One is a passage from Sam Altman’s blog in 2013. He had heard a saying from Qi Lu: successful people create companies, more successful people create countries, and the most successful people create religions. Altman drew his own conclusion: the most successful founders “are on a mission to create something closer to a religion”, and at some point a company turns out to be the easiest way to do it.

Hao comes back to it in chapter 18, where she argues that OpenAI’s mission works as a formula for empire: it gathers talent, it gathers capital, and it is vague enough to be reinterpreted at will. In chapter 10 she writes that the people who fear AGI and the people who long for it preach from the same bible. For her, the religious quality of the AI labs is the warning sign.

I read the same sentence as a forecast, and an accurate one. A company has always held people together with two things: what it pays them for and what it lets them believe. For most of industrial history the first carried the weight. The work was the reason to show up, the wage was the reason to stay, and the mission statement was decoration. If AI makes a great deal of human work cheaper, the first bond weakens. What is left to hold a group of people together is the second: a shared idea of what they are building and why it matters.

That is not new. Monasteries, guilds, universities, and the early labs of the nuclear age were held together this way, and they built things no wage alone would have bought. The OpenAI that Hao describes runs on the same fuel: people who took less money than Google offered because they believed in the mission, and who threatened to leave together when they thought it was in danger. Altman put a line from Admiral Rickover on the office walls for the same reason (One person can make a difference).

Hao is right that a belief can be bent to serve power, and that a vague mission can be reinterpreted to justify almost anything. That is the risk of every religion. But the answer is to look at what the faith builds and whom it serves, not to wish companies were held together by wages alone. I expect more of them to look like this, not fewer, and I share some of the faith myself: An emergent property of matter.

More on the book in my review, An Empire of People.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), epigraph, chapter 10, “Gods and Demons”, and chapter 18, “A Formula for Empire”.
  • Sam Altman, Successful People, blog post, March 7, 2013.

entry.title: One person can make a difference
entry.content:
In the early days of OpenAI, Sam Altman had a quote painted on the office walls. It comes from Hyman G. Rickover, the admiral known as the father of the nuclear navy, who built the first nuclear-powered submarines:

I believe it is the duty of each of us to act as if the fate of the world depended on him. Admittedly, one man by himself cannot do the job. However, one man can make a difference.

Karen Hao tells the story in Empire of AI (chapter 6). Years later Altman put the same quote, with a few more lines about each person’s “individual and independent capacities”, at the end of a memo to the company. The memo asked for less transparency, at least one impressive demonstration of progress a year, and more seriousness and unity. Under the quote he wrote: “We must put the mission ahead of any individual preferences.”

I like the quote, and I believe it. It is the conviction behind most things worth building, and it is the same thing I argued about who carries progress: a small number of people deciding to act as if it depends on them is how a lot of the future gets made. Rickover is a fair example. A nuclear navy was a state project, but it happened at the pace it did because one difficult man drove it.

What strikes me is the turn in the memo. Rickover’s lines are about the individual: each of us, our own capacities, our own duty. Altman uses them to ask each person to set their own judgement aside for the mission. Both can be true at once, a person can make a difference by joining something larger, but the second reading is the one that makes an organisation dangerous when the mission is as large as the one OpenAI claimed. If everyone acts as if the fate of the world depends on them, someone still has to be allowed to say that the fate of the world is not in fact at stake this quarter.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 6. Hao prints the quote with gender-neutral brackets; the wording above follows the version usually attributed to Rickover.
  • Hyman G. Rickover, attributed to “Thoughts on Man’s Purpose in Life” (1974), as given on Quotepark after Wikiquote. I have not seen the primary text.

entry.title: A billion without a plan
entry.content:
One passage in Karen Hao’s Empire of AI (chapter 5) stays with me more than the chapters around it. In early 2023 a Chinese AI researcher tells her that what OpenAI did could only have happened in Silicon Valley. China has the talent, he says, but no team there would have been given a billion dollars, let alone ten, for an expensive technology without a clear picture of what it would become and what it would be good for. Chinese money followed only after ChatGPT showed there was revenue to be had. Hao takes it one step further: not even Google or DeepMind put open-ended sums into scaling before ChatGPT. It took OpenAI specifically, with its “billionaire origins”, its ideology, and Sam Altman’s fundraising.

Hao uses this against OpenAI’s claim that AGI was inevitable, and she is right on that point. Nothing about it was inevitable. But I read the same fact as a statement about capital. The bet that produced large language models was made before there was a business case, by a small number of people who controlled a lot of money and understood the technology well enough to want it. A committee, a state plan, or a listed company answering to its next quarter would each have asked the question the Chinese researcher’s investors asked, and each would have said no.

That is what concentrated capital is good at. A market economy lets a few people allocate large sums on conviction, and most of those bets fail. The ones that work fund things no consensus process would have chosen. I argue about this often with people who see Silicon Valley’s founders and investors as the problem. I do not think they are villains. They are allocators, some of them unusually good at it, and over the long run economies that reward effective allocation of resources have produced more than economies that plan them. Whether the bet was a good one for everyone else is a separate question, and Hao’s book is mostly about that question.

Two things keep me honest about this:

  • The billionaire origin was more promise than cash. Hao reports (chapter 2) that of the billion dollars pledged at OpenAI’s founding, the lab received only around $130 million, less than $45 million of it from Elon Musk. The pledge bought credibility and talent. The money that paid for scale came later, from Microsoft, a company deciding by very different means.
  • Concentration cuts both ways. The same structure that funds a bet without a plan also leaves the costs of that bet, the data, the labour, the energy, to be decided by the same few people. That is the part of the argument I have not resolved.

The broader argument, about who carries progress and why what they build spreads, is in who carries progress.

Related: allocation is the same act at every scale, a person, a family, and a bank all betting on the future with limited means.

entry.title: Who carries progress
entry.content:
A colleague with a philosophical bent and I had the same argument from opposite ends recently. He distrusts the founders and investors of Silicon Valley, and he holds that the real breakthroughs in science and technology come from academia, and so in the end from the state that funds it. I argued the opposite: progress is carried by people who have to make things work. Entrepreneurs, investors, and companies.

My reasoning goes like this. Someone who has to make a venture survive is selected for the qualities progress needs: being effective, being efficient, daring to try what nobody has asked for. A market does not only reward those qualities once. It trains them, in the people and in the organisations they build, because the ones without them run out of money. An academic can be right for decades without anyone depending on the result. An entrepreneur finds out within a year or two. That feedback loop is the same one I trust when I measure intelligence by what it does rather than by what it knows.

The second half of the argument is the one I care about more. Over the long run, what these people build does not stay with them. Know-how leaks: employees leave and start their own companies, techniques get published or reverse engineered, tools get cheaper until anyone can use them. The sum of many self-interested builders ends up democratising what each of them tried to keep. Large language models are the latest case. A billion dollars bet without a plan became, within a few years, something a single person can run on a laptop.

My colleague has real evidence on his side, and I should say so. The deep learning that OpenAI scaled came out of university labs, Geoffrey Hinton’s in Toronto among them. The web was invented at CERN, a publicly funded laboratory, and Tim Berners-Lee chose to give it away. Where I still disagree is on what counts as the breakthrough. Academia often finds the idea. It usually takes someone with money at risk to turn it into something that reaches everyone, and the Transformer, invented at Google, shows that the line between the two is not as clean as either of us made it sound.

None of this makes me a capitalist in the sense my colleague meant. I am closer to the geolibertarian, or left-libertarian, tradition: Henry George and Silvio Gesell, and in our time Hillel Steiner, Peter Vallentyne, and Philippe Van Parijs. In that tradition you own yourself and what you make, but land and natural resources belong to everyone, and their value should be shared, through a land value tax or a basic income. It fits the argument above. Know-how disperses on its own; land and resources do not, and that is where the sharing has to be designed. And if AI takes us anywhere near post-scarcity, we will have to revisit those designs soon, because the question will no longer be who produces the most, but who owns what is still scarce.

Open threads:

  • Is there a fair test of who carries progress, or does each side count the breakthroughs that suit it?
  • How fast does know-how actually diffuse, and what slows it down: patents, secrecy, scale, compute?
  • What remains scarce when production is cheap, and who should own it?

entry.title: Citizen entrepreneurs
entry.content:
A friend of mine, an enterprise architect at a large Swiss energy group, answers the tumult in between with the observation that the same tools that threaten jobs make citizen entrepreneurs possible. An ordinary person can use AI to identify a business opportunity, use AI to build the business, and use AI to operate it. The barrier was never only money; it was the ten different competences a business needs on day one, and those are now available by the hour. The operating half is already true for infrastructure, where one person can now run what used to take a team, as I argued in How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again. He took his own idea seriously enough to build a business idea factory, a system that generates and evaluates opportunities. About a week before we talked, someone else announced a project with the same shape on Hacker News, which he took as confirmation rather than competition.

I find it the most hopeful reading of the window, and the one with the most work in it. It assumes the capability really is democratised, which I believe, and it assumes people will take it up, which is the part the window is for.
